summary:
A trans visitor to South Carolina enters under the United States federal document regime before state law applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issuing new passports only as M or F, while previously issued X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad. Entry screening adds exposure: the State Department flags visa applicants with an internal marking and treats a declared gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud with a permanent bar.

Facilities are the sharpest state-level exposure. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The law takes a restriction that already applied in school settings and extends it across campus settings in higher education. The ACLU of South Carolina issued its response on 18 May 2026, describing the measure as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education and noting that the Senate amended the bill before passage.

Custody carries a separate documented restriction. South Carolina operates a freeze-frame policy that limits the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated, an in-prison treatment restriction rather than a housing-placement rule. Transgender prisoners nationally have reported denied care, and the Federal Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment ranks states by reading bills for the severity of adult and youth law. On the strength of the university expansion, South Carolina sits among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier, so the state's position is rising faster than its current tier suggests.

The freeze-frame treatment policy is shared with three other states, Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah, according to the Transitics tracker cited by Metro Weekly on 11 July 2026. Four jurisdictions out of the country holding such policies places South Carolina in a minority group, but one that rights trackers are actively monitoring.

Bathroom restrictions applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory nationally, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement elsewhere has produced arrests: in April 2025 a trans student was handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, an incident civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. South Carolina's law covers schools and campuses rather than public buildings generally.
localsOnly:
Transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities must use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth under House Bill 4756, signed 15 May 2026 and amended by the Senate before passage. The ACLU of South Carolina, responding on 18 May 2026, frames the requirement as discrimination affecting both K-12 and higher-education students.

Transgender people incarcerated in South Carolina are subject to a freeze-frame policy restricting the treatments they may receive during imprisonment. The restriction governs treatment rather than where a prisoner is housed.

South Carolina residents remain bound by the federal identity-document rules: state-side changes to a name or gender marker do not alter what a passport or visa will show, and federal offices must use sex rather than gender in their records.
outOfScopeNotes:
No South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, or solitary or segregation for transgender prisoners is recorded in the sources assembled here; that question remains unresolved rather than settled either way.

The specific treatments barred or frozen under the South Carolina freeze-frame policy are not itemised in the sources reviewed, so the precise scope of medical restriction for an incarcerated trans person is unresolved.

Enforcement of House Bill 4756 is not documented here: the sources record the signing, the amendment and the objection, but not penalties, complaint procedures or any reported campus incident under the law.

South Carolina-specific rules on changing a gender marker on a state driver's licence or birth certificate are not sourced in this inventory; the wider pattern of state document closure, including Kansas legislation in March 2026, is documented but not tied to South Carolina.

The July 2026 risk-assessment tiering reflects a reading of bills and enacted text rather than measured enforcement, so the ranking should be treated as a legislative indicator.
